sections.title: What is DP on Graphs?
sections.content:
**DP on graphs** means defining states over graph nodes and transitions over edges. The critical requirement: the graph must be a **DAG** (Directed Acyclic Graph) for standard DP to apply. DP requires filling states in some valid order - you must compute a state's value before computing any state that depends on it. A topological ordering of the DAG gives exactly this valid order. Cycles prevent any such ordering from existing, making naive DP fail or loop infinitely.

Two main patterns arise. In **DAG DP**, you compute answers directly over the graph's structure - counting paths, finding the longest or shortest path, or computing some aggregate over all paths from source to target. In **DP with extended state**, you augment the node with additional information to create a state-space graph that is a DAG even when the original graph has cycles. For example, `(node, steps_taken)` or `(node, visited_bitmask)` creates states that only move forward and never revisit the same state.

The connection to shortest-path algorithms is deep. Dijkstra's algorithm is DP on a graph where the state is `(node, current_min_distance)` and the priority queue ensures states are processed in optimal order. Bellman-Ford is DP where each of K iterations relaxes all edges - `dp[node][k]` is the minimum cost path using at most `k` edges. Understanding graph DP as a generalization of these classical algorithms makes it easier to adapt them to new constraints.

A particularly powerful extension is **bitmask DP on graphs**, where the state `(node, visited_mask)` tracks which nodes have been visited. This encodes the entire history of the path in a compact integer. For `n ≤ 20` nodes, there are `n × 2^n` states - feasible in time and memory - enabling optimal solutions to otherwise NP-hard problems like the Traveling Salesman Problem.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Use graph DP when the problem involves counting or optimizing paths in a directed graph, with possible constraints on the number of steps or which nodes have been visited. If the graph is a DAG (or can be processed as one via topological sort), DAG DP applies. If paths have bounded length (at most k edges), the Bellman-Ford style k-step DP applies. If n is small (≤ 20) and you need to visit all nodes optimally, bitmask DP applies.
signals: number of paths from source to target in DAG
longest path in a directed graph
cheapest flight with at most k stops
number of ways to reach destination
paths with bounded steps or cost

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
## DAG DP

Compute topological order of the DAG first (Kahn's algorithm or DFS-based). Then iterate nodes in topological order. For each node, compute `dp[node]` from all its predecessors' dp values.

- **Count paths**: `dp[node] = sum(dp[prev])` for all predecessors
- **Longest path**: `dp[node] = max(dp[prev] + 1)` for all predecessors  
- **Shortest path with uniform weights**: BFS order is equivalent to topological order here

Base case: `dp[source] = 1` for count (one way to start), or `0` for shortest path (zero cost at source).

## Bounded-Step DP (Bellman-Ford Variant)

`dp[node][k]` = optimal cost to reach `node` using **at most** `k` edges. Iterate `k` from 1 to K. For each k, iterate all edges `(u, v, w)`: `dp[v][k] = min(dp[v][k-1], dp[u][k-1] + w)`. Base: `dp[source][0] = 0`, all others Infinity.

Critical: copy the previous DP array before each k-iteration (`prev = [...dp[k-1]]`) and read from `prev` when updating `dp[k]`. Without this, updates within the same k-step propagate through multiple edges in one pass, violating the k-step constraint.

## State Space Graph (Extended State)

When the graph has cycles but the problem has a parameter that strictly increases (steps taken, nodes visited), create a state `(node, parameter)`. This state space is always a DAG because the parameter only increases. Apply standard DAG DP on the state space.

Example: `dp[node][steps]` for 'minimum cost path with exactly k steps' - transitions increase steps by 1, so no state cycles.

## Bitmask DP on Graphs

`dp[mask][node]` = minimum cost to have visited exactly the nodes in `mask`, currently at `node`. Transition: for each unvisited node `next` (bit not set in mask): `dp[mask | (1 << next)][next] = min(dp[mask][next], dp[mask][node] + dist[node][next])`.

Base: `dp[1 << start][start] = 0`. Answer for TSP: `min(dp[fullMask][node] + dist[node][start])` over all `node`. States: `n × 2^n`. Feasible for n ≤ 20.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: DAG DP integrates topological sort with DP fill - as each node becomes reachable (in-degree hits 0), propagate its dp value to successors. Bounded-step DP copies the previous state before each iteration to prevent multi-hop updates within the same step count - this is the most common bug in this pattern.

items.name: Memoized DFS on DAG (Top-Down)
items.description: Instead of computing topological order explicitly, use recursive DFS with memoization. When visiting a node, recursively solve all its successors, cache the result. Works naturally on DAGs since no cycles means no infinite recursion. Often cleaner to write than Kahn's-based bottom-up.
items.example_problem: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix

items.name: TSP with Bitmask DP
items.description: dp[mask][node] = minimum cost visiting exactly the nodes in mask, ending at node. Transition adds one unvisited node at a time. O(n² × 2^n) time. Feasible for n ≤ 20. The full mask (all 1s) gives the answer - add return cost to source.

items.name: Probability DP on Graphs
items.description: dp[node] = probability of reaching this node from source. Transition: dp[v] += dp[u] × prob(u→v). Works on DAGs in topological order. For graphs with cycles, convert to a system of equations or use iterative methods.

items.name: Shortest Path DP Connection
items.description: Dijkstra's is DP where states are (node, current_distance) processed in priority order. Bellman-Ford is DP with k-step iterations. Floyd-Warshall is DP where dp[k][i][j] = shortest path from i to j using only nodes 0..k as intermediaries. Understanding these as DP unifies shortest-path algorithms.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(V+E) for DAG DP, O(K×E) for bounded-step, O(n² × 2^n) for bitmask DP
sections.space: O(V) for DAG DP, O(V) for bounded-step (rolling), O(n × 2^n) for bitmask
sections.explanation: DAG DP processes each vertex and edge once in topological order: O(V + E). Bounded-step DP runs K iterations each processing all E edges: O(K × E). Bitmask DP has n × 2^n states with n transitions each: O(n² × 2^n) time and O(n × 2^n) space. For n=20: 20M states × 20 transitions = 400M operations - borderline feasible with fast constant. For n=25: 25 × 33M = 800M states - generally infeasible.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Applying DAG DP to a graph with cycles - cycles create infinite dependencies; the DP has no valid fill order and either infinite-loops or produces wrong answers; always verify the graph is a DAG or use Bellman-Ford / memoized DFS with cycle detection instead.

Wrong topological order direction - must process nodes BEFORE their successors; processing in reverse topological order (successors before predecessors) means dp[successor] isn't ready when dp[node] tries to use it.

Not copying the dp array before each k-step iteration in bounded-step DP - `prev[u]` must reflect values from k-1 steps, not the current k-step's partially-updated values; without copying, a path u→v→w can be applied in a single k=1 iteration, giving k=2 reachability.
Bitmask DP exponential blowup - 2^20 = ~1M is feasible, 2^25 = ~33M starts hitting memory limits, 2^30 = ~1B is infeasible; always check that n ≤ 20 before attempting bitmask DP.

Confusing longest path in a DAG (solvable in O(V+E) with DP) with longest path in a general graph (NP-hard) - the DAG constraint is what makes it tractable; remove it and the problem becomes computationally intractable.

items.title: Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination
items.why: Combines Dijkstra's shortest path with DAG DP count - count paths achieving the minimum distance, using the shortest-path DAG as the underlying structure.

items.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
items.why: Direct bounded-step DP - tests the critical 'copy prev before updating' pattern and the K+1 iteration count.

items.title: Count All Possible Routes
items.why: Top-down memoized DP on a graph with bounded fuel - state is (city, fuel_remaining), transitions reduce fuel, tests memoization on a non-tree graph.

items.title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
items.why: Memoized DFS on an implicit DAG - the increasing constraint ensures no cycles, making the grid a DAG where dp[cell] = longest path starting at that cell.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: Graph DP introduced the idea of encoding visited nodes as a bitmask state. Bitmask DP formalizes this into a full technique - representing any subset of n elements as a binary integer and DP-ing over all 2^n subsets. It extends graph DP to assignment, covering, and optimal sequencing problems.
